title: Reward-Modulated STDP
intro: STDP is unsupervised: it strengthens whatever fires together, useful or not. Animals learn from consequences that arrive later, such as a reward a second after the action that earned it. Reward-modulated STDP (R-STDP) is a three-factor rule. Pre- and postsynaptic timing (factors one and two) only tag a synapse as eligible, and a global neuromodulatory signal such as dopamine (factor three) decides whether, and in which direction, the tag becomes a real weight change.

blocks.source:
dc/dt = -c / tau_c + STDP(Delta t) delta(t - t_pre/post)    eligibility trace, per synapse
dw/dt = c(t) * d(t)                                          weight follows trace times dopamine
dd/dt = -d / tau_d + DA(t)                                   dopamine: global, phasic bursts at reward

tau_c is about 1 s, tau_d about 0.2 s

blocks.text: Each pre/post pairing adds the usual STDP amount to the synapse's eligibility trace c instead of to its weight. The trace decays over about a second. When dopamine arrives, every synapse with a nonzero trace changes in proportion to c times d. Synapses that were active just before the reward are credited. Synapses active long before, or never, are not. A negative modulator, a dip below baseline dopamine, can likewise turn eligible potentiation into depression.

This is how R-STDP tackles the distal reward or temporal credit assignment problem: the trace bridges the gap between a millisecond-scale spike coincidence and a reward that comes seconds later. In Izhikevich's simulations, a network of 1000 neurons learned to strengthen the one synapse whose pre-post pairing was followed by a delayed reward, out of 100,000 synapses firing at random.

widget.title: Eligibility trace meets a delayed reward

items: The pairing happens at 0.1 s. Move the reward delay from 0 to 3000 ms. The weight change falls off roughly exponentially with delay (about 1.7 to 0.6 to 0.08 here): the trace has to still be there when dopamine arrives.
Shorten tau_c to 200 ms with a 1 s delay. The trace is gone before the reward and nothing is learned. The trace's time constant sets how far back in time credit can reach.

Lengthen tau_c to 3 s. Learning tolerates longer delays, but in a busy network more irrelevant synapses also stay eligible, so credit becomes less precise. That is the core trade-off of eligibility traces.

Reward prediction error. Use d = reward - expected reward instead of raw reward, the temporal-difference error carried by dopamine neurons (Schultz, Dayan & Montague 1997). Frémaux, Sprekeler and Gerstner (2010) showed this is necessary: with raw reward, R-STDP drifts unless the reward is centered.

Policy-gradient rules. Florian (2007) and Pfister et al. (2006) derived reward-modulated rules that perform gradient ascent on expected reward for stochastic spiking neurons. R-STDP is a biologically motivated approximation.

Other third factors. Acetylcholine, noradrenaline and serotonin, and also top-down attention or surprise signals, act as gates in the same mathematical framework (Frémaux & Gerstner 2016; Gerstner et al. 2018).

Learning in hardware. Three-factor rules suit neuromorphic chips because the third factor is a single broadcast value. Intel's Loihi supports programmable rules with traces and reward-like modulatory inputs.
Unbalanced STDP plus constant positive reward is just Hebbian learning with extra steps. Center the reward.
Eligibility traces need memory per synapse: one extra state variable each.
Exploration matters. If the network never produces the rewarded pattern, there is nothing to reinforce, so stochastic neurons or injected noise help.

blocks.text: For a cortical column: the Thousand Brains Theory learns mostly without reward, since columns model the world through prediction. But a column that drives behavior, such as choosing where to move a sensor next, needs a reinforcement signal. A practical design is local unsupervised rules (STDP, dendritic prediction learning) inside the column, plus an R-STDP pathway from the column's output to a small action-selection population, with the reward or prediction error as a broadcast third factor.

Sources: Izhikevich, E. M. (2007), "Solving the distal reward problem through linkage of STDP and dopamine signaling", Cerebral Cortex 17:2443-2452. Frémaux, N., Sprekeler, H. & Gerstner, W. (2010), "Functional requirements for reward-modulated spike-timing-dependent plasticity", Journal of Neuroscience 30:13326-13337. Frémaux, N. & Gerstner, W. (2016), "Neuromodulated spike-timing-dependent plasticity, and theory of three-factor learning rules", Frontiers in Neural Circuits 9:85. Florian, R. V. (2007), Neural Computation 19:1468-1502. Schultz, W., Dayan, P. & Montague, P. R. (1997), Science 275:1593-1599. Gerstner, W., Lehmann, M., Liakoni, V., Corneil, D. & Brea, J. (2018), Frontiers in Neural Circuits 12:53.
